  * Microsoft is improving Windows Release Notes. For more information, please see What's next for Windows release notes.

  * Customers running Windows Server 2008 R2, or Windows Server 2008 need to purchase the Extended Security Update to continue receiving security updates. See 4522133 for more information.

## State of the art: what the attacks and benchmarks show

The case that prompt injection is a production breach risk, not a lab curiosity, rests on named, dated, disclosed incidents against systems built by the most capable engineering organizations in the world. We walk through four, because each isolates a different leg of the trifecta and a different lesson.

### EchoLeak: zero-click exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot

In June 2025, Microsoft disclosed and patched CVE-2025-32711, an indirect prompt injection vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot that researchers at Aim Security named EchoLeak. It carried a CVSS score of 9.3, and it is widely described as the first real-world zero-click prompt injection exploit against a production LLM system ^{[6]}. Zero-click is the operative word. The attack required no action from the victim beyond having an attacker's email present in their mailbox. The email contained instructions addressed to Copilot, hidden in ordinary-looking content. When the user later asked Copilot a normal question, the assistant, in the course of summarizing across the user's mailbox and documents, read the attacker's instructions and followed them, accessing internal files and transmitting their contents to an attacker-controlled endpoint ^{[7]}.

# Microsoft 365 Copilot ‘zero-click’ vulnerability enabled data exfiltration

June 11, 2025

By Laura French

Image: (Credit: vladim_ka – stock.adobe.com)

(Credit: vladim_ka – stock.adobe.com)

Microsoft patched a “zero-click” flaw in its Microsoft 365 Copilot retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tool that could have allowed for exfiltration of sensitive data, according to Aim Security.

The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2025-32711, which has a critical CVSS score of 9.3, Aim Security told SC Media in an email. Microsoft said in its disclosure that the AI command injection vulnerability has not been exploited in the wild and requires no further user action to resolve.

The flaw, dubbed “EchoLeak,” would have allowed an attacker to extract potentially sensitive information from a user’s connected Microsoft 365 services, such as their Outlook email, OneDrive storage, Office files, SharePoint sites and Microsoft Teams chat history, by sending a specially crafted email that bypasses several security measures, Aim Security explained.

But there was no in-the-wild incident that fit the canonical shape of the threat: a remote, unauthenticated attacker, no user interaction required, full privilege escalation across the LLM's trust boundary.

That moment ended on June 11, 2025, when Aim Security published the technical disclosure of EchoLeak.^{[1]}

EchoLeak was not novel in any individual mechanism it employed. Indirect prompt injection had been described by Greshake et al. in 2023.^{[2]} Markdown-link exfiltration had been documented in toy systems for over a year. The use of trusted-domain proxies to bypass content security policy was a well-understood SSRF pattern. What made EchoLeak the inflection point was that it was the first time these mechanisms had been chained together against a production AI system used by hundreds of millions of enterprise users — and that the chain had worked.^{[3]}

The technical story of EchoLeak is interesting in its own right. The reason this analysis exists is that the structural story is more important than the technical one, and the structural story has been less clearly told. The patch closed the bug. It did not close the vulnerability class. Engineers who treat EchoLeak as a Microsoft incident, rather than a category-defining moment for AI-integrated systems, will be exposed to the next instance of the same class on whatever platform they ship next.

What follows is an attempt to explain, with the level of precision a senior engineer needs, what actually happened, why each defense was structurally insufficient, and what an effective defense looks like — not for Copilot specifically, but for any RAG-based AI system in production.

Researchers at Aim Security disclosed a Microsoft Copilot vulnerability of critical severity this week that could have enabled sensitive data exfiltration via prompt injection attacks.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

June 12, 2025

3 Min Read

Image: Microsoft software product logos with Copilot in the center

Source: Adrian Vidal via Alamy Stock Photo

A critical vulnerability could have enabled attackers to unleash prompt injection attacks against Copilot users, though Microsoft ultimately addressed the issue before it went public.

Aim Security, a firm that sells security tools in the AI product space, published research Wednesday regarding "EchoLeak," a zero-click vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2025-32711, targeting Microsoft 365 Copilot. According to researchers at the vendor's Aim Labs, attack chains involving the vulnerability "allow attackers to automatically exfiltrate sensitive and proprietary information from M365 Copilot context, without the user's awareness, or relying on any specific victim behavior."
